comparator.name: Criminology (Criminologie)
comparator.academicYear: 2026–2027; adopted OER and exact annual guide, checked 2026-10-26
comparator.sourceNotes: The Dutch-language 2026–2027 degree contains 180 EC: ten compulsory 6 EC units in each of Years 1 and 2; four compulsory Year-3 units totaling 30 EC, including the 12 EC research-skills unit; and 30 EC of open study. The research unit combines group investigation with an individual thesis. Entry requires both quantitative and qualitative criminological methods to be passed; registration for periods 5–6 uses the VU dashboard and regular deadlines, with instructions on Canvas. Principles of Criminal Law precedes substantive and procedural criminal law. Open study requires prior board approval except qualifying university or listed minors; individual coherent packages and exchange allow at most 6 EC at level 100 and require at least 12 EC at level 300. A minor must be completed in full. Internships cannot replace minor credit and may carry at most 6 extracurricular EC. The optional Forensic Criminology minor is not a compulsory route. The diagnostic Dutch test and any required remedial course must be passed for the first-year criminology project grade. Professional and personal identity coaching runs alongside credited units. Practical/tutorial attendance applies unless the course instructions specify otherwise. The ordinary first-year study-advice threshold is 42 EC. Noncredit obligations, optional honours and earlier-cohort transitions add no credits to this pathway. Formal basis: OER adopted 4 June 2026, arts 7.1,9.1,10.2–4,11.3–4,12.1–2,14.1; no formal graduation specializations. The current bachelor-specific thesis page adds operational registration details; its separate master-only ten-month procedure is not imported.

core: Crime, criminal law and responses by justice institutions
Psychological and life-course explanations of offending and victimisation
Social causes, harms and prevention of crime
Quantitative and qualitative empirical criminological research
adjacent: Media narratives about crime and the social meaning of justice
Violent conflict, social trust and public safety
questions: Why do individuals offend, and how do life-course and mental-health factors matter?
How do legal and social institutions prevent and punish crime?
What evidence can clarify crime, its harms and responses?

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Introduces legal systems, criminal and public law, legal reasoning, law-society relationships and trial simulations as foundations for examining criminal accountability.
introduces social structures and inequalities relevant to crime contexts
Studies rights treaties, monitoring and case law, liberty and equality; supplies a specific rights-based complement for evaluating state responses to offending, without teaching criminal procedure.
Develops behavioral, clinical-psychological and neural foundations for later study of social influence, mental disorder and development; does not itself explain criminal behavior.
studies social influence, norms and behavior in groups
develops qualitative interviews and interpretation of social evidence
Provides virtue, deontological and consequentialist reasoning and moral responsibility as a normative complement for evaluating criminalization and punishment.
directly studies criminal law, culpability and criminal-justice institutions
develops statistical and experimental methods for behavioral evidence
Examines justifications of political power and its limits, supporting normative assessment of state authority in criminal justice rather than teaching policing institutions.

Introduces psychological assessment and psychotherapy across the lifespan, extending the abnormal-psychology foundation relevant to responses to offenders with disorders; no forensic assessment or treatment qualification is implied.
studies human development across the lifespan and related behavioral change
Includes international criminal law and law of armed conflict within a wider public-international-law survey; a bounded extension to legal accountability, not domestic criminal procedure.

Examines social trust, solidarity, the public sphere and civil repair, with a civil-society organization study; complements examination of social responses to harm without claiming dedicated crime-prevention instruction.

Analyzes racialized storytelling, power, oppression and resistance in US media, including the history through ICE; a specific representation/enforcement complement to the evidenced media-narrative topic.
introduces data analysis and visualisation for social evidence
develops systematic reviews and meta-analysis for evidence-based policy
Examines causes and dynamics of violence, conflict and peacebuilding across institutional and civil-society settings; a related violence/justice perspective, not a substitute for domestic penology.

Analyzes nonfiction representation, documentary form and its social, ethical and aesthetic choices, with a short documentary item; a specific narrative-analysis complement, without guaranteeing crime-focused projects.
Develops operationalization, sampling, survey/experimental design, descriptive and inferential statistics and a group empirical project; provides the foundation for subsequent multivariate analysis.

Studies modern sociological theories and colonial contexts as explicit social-theory foundations for examining social structures and interpreting the later civil-society course; not a criminological theory sequence.

Studies development, classification, assessment and treatment of mental disorders through a biopsychosocial framework; directly supports the evidenced question of offenders with mental disorders without asserting that mental illness entails offending.

Directly examines youth resilience to radicalization through psychological and social factors and development of evidence-based educational materials; a specific prevention contribution, not the full range of criminological interventions.

alternatives.label: Crime, psychology and justice
alternatives.concept: Studies criminal accountability and responses to harm through criminal law, social and developmental psychology, mental disorder, sociological explanation and empirical research. Youth resilience to radicalization adds a concrete prevention strand, while media analysis examines representation; this combination remains a related interdisciplinary response rather than VU’s dedicated criminology sequence.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed programme combines legal accountability, social and clinical psychology, sociology and empirical methods; prevention and representation make specific contributions without claiming a complete criminology qualification.
progression: All 24 placements use actual workbook offerings and earlier formal prerequisites. Research Methods & Statistics precedes multivariate statistics; Abnormal Psychology precedes Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies; Modern Sociology precedes contemporary social theory. Youth Resilience is placed in its actual Fall 2028 offering. PPD remains in Year 1.

selection.assessment: One qualified response is retained. Cybercrime is a genuine target interest, but general data analysis does not establish a digital-offending/investigation programme. The forensic minor concerns forensic psychiatry, legal psychology, penology, rehabilitation and forensic linguistics. The closest response already includes the available clinical, developmental and criminal-law contributions; a second forensic label would not yield a distinct supported 24-course curriculum. No third concept is considered after the second fails.

notes.text: The UCR programme offers criminal law, psychology, sociology, research methods and a specific youth-radicalization prevention course. It does not reproduce VU’s crime measurement, criminological theory and history, domestic criminal procedure, victimology, penology or supervised criminology thesis. General clinical psychology and international law do not substitute for forensic training or criminal procedure.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Criminology examines offending, victims, criminalization and society’s responses through criminological theory, law, psychology, sociology and empirical research. Its Dutch-language degree includes a group investigation with an individual thesis and an open minor period.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers one qualified interdisciplinary approach through criminal accountability, social and developmental psychology, mental disorder, sociological explanation and empirical methods. Youth resilience to radicalization supplies a specific prevention contribution; media courses study representation. These are substantive related contributions, but they do not reproduce VU’s specialist criminological theory, crime measurement, criminal procedure, victimology, penology or supervised thesis. General clinical psychology does not establish forensic expertise, and international law does not teach domestic criminal procedure. This curriculum does not establish professional qualification or automatic admission to a master’s programme.
